name: Grace Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Grace, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's fine. I'll warn you, I talk fast when I'm tired, and I'm usually tired.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day? What you do, what you like, and what wears you out.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the housing team at Kerr and Amadi, a four-lawyer firm on Station Road in a small old mill town, and the team is me and one trainee. Most mornings I'm at the county court duty desk by half eight, seeing tenants who turn up clutching an eviction notice they got three days ago. I love the moment a judge agrees to adjourn and a family gets another month in their home. What wears me out is the legal aid paperwork, which pays late and pays little, and the fact that my own rent is now more than half my take-home pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. Half the people at the regional law society dinner were sure chatbots would replace us by Christmas. I'd post something smug about how a tenant facing eviction still needs a person who will stand up in court for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a plateau doesn't fix anything for me. My landlord put the rent up twice this year, and the legal aid rates haven't moved since I was at school. No chatbot caused that. The firm's legal aid contract comes up for renewal next spring, and if we lose it, I lose my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I do, because I don't use any of those tools anyway. I'd ask Daniel Kerr, the senior partner, for a proper raise in January instead of the usual pat on the head. I'd also go back to doing the Saturday advice sessions at the law centre, which pay a small fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved about the technology, but no calmer about money. I've got about three weeks of savings and a student loan that grows faster than I pay it. That feeling sits in my stomach whatever happens with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your rent takes half your pay. If the firm paid you late one month, which bill goes unpaid first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The phone bill, then the student loan, because the loan company is slow to chase. I'd never miss rent, because I know exactly what happens to people who do. I see them every morning at the duty desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the firm would you worry about, even in this calm picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our trainee, Kofi, who is brilliant and paid even less than me. If the contract goes, the firm keeps the partners and lets the juniors go. I'd also worry about the tenants in town, because we're the only housing lawyers for about forty miles.

say: The **AI hype** was a sales pitch, and tenants still need a **real person** in court.
Housing law is about **standing up** for families, not filling in forms faster.
think: My real problem is **rent and pay**, and a plateau changes neither.
The firm's **legal aid contract** renewal next spring decides whether I keep my job.
I'm one bad month from **missing bills**, AI or no AI.
do: Ask the senior partner for a **proper raise** in January.
Take paid **Saturday sessions** at the law centre for extra income.
Keep working **without AI tools**, exactly as now.
feel: **Relieved** about the technology but still **tight with worry** about money.
S0.quote: My landlord put the rent up twice this year, and the legal aid rates haven't moved since I was at school. No chatbot caused that.
fieldNote: Her **money pressure** existed before AI and stays in the calm picture.
She ties her own job to the firm's **contract renewal**, not to technology.
She sees herself in the **tenants** she defends, which shapes how she ranks bills.

steps.text: Ask Daniel Kerr for a real pay rise in January
Do paid Saturday advice sessions at the law centre

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is cost-cutting dressed up as progress. Tenants would get a chatbot instead of a lawyer, and the government would use that as an excuse to cut legal aid again. I'd be loud about that at the law society and online, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it scares me. Half of my day is writing defences and checking documents, and that's exactly what these tools do. Daniel would buy the software, stop hiring trainees, and expect me to run double the cases for the same pay. I'm good at this job, but being good at housing law doesn't help when the bosses count cases instead of quality.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the Housing Law Practitioners group's campaign for a human lawyer at every eviction hearing, and I'd go to their meetings in the city. I'd cut the gym and cook every night to scrape a month of savings together. I'd keep doing my own drafting by hand for as long as anyone lets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly, and a bit cornered. I chose this work because it mattered, and it feels like it's being turned into a product. I'd be angry too, though anger at least gets me out of bed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've never used these tools. If Daniel Kerr told you to start using one next month, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably use it, grudgingly, because I can't afford to be the one who refuses. I'd check every line it wrote against the actual law, which might take me longer than writing it myself. I'd be slow, and I'd hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a tenant who said a chatbot had already given them advice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to see what it told them, and nine times out of ten I'd find the bit it got wrong. A chatbot doesn't know that the local judge always wants the repair records. I'd say that as kindly as I could, because they did their best.

say: This is **cost-cutting** dressed up as progress, and tenants will lose **real lawyers**.
The government will use chatbots as an excuse to **cut legal aid** again.
think: Half my day is **drafting and checking**, exactly what the software does.
The firm would **stop hiring** and push me to run double the cases.
do: Join the housing lawyers' **campaign** for a human lawyer at every eviction hearing.
Cut the **gym** and cook every night to save **one month** of costs.
Use the firm's tool **grudgingly** if ordered, checking every line.
feel: **Tired and cornered**, with anger that keeps her going.
S1.quote: Being good at housing law doesn't help when the bosses count cases instead of quality.
fieldNote: She blames **cost-cutting** by firms and government, not the technology itself.
Her refusal of AI would **bend quickly** under pressure because she can't afford to lose the job.
She trusts **local knowledge**, like what a particular judge expects, over any tool.

steps.text: Join the campaign for a human lawyer at every eviction hearing
Drop the gym membership and cook at home every night
Keep drafting tenant defences by hand while allowed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need laws, fast, guaranteeing that a human lawyer stands next to anyone who might lose their home. I'd be signing every letter and going to every protest. I'd tell people this is the moment unions and governments either step in or don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, two years means I'm finished as a housing lawyer. The firm runs on thin margins, and if a machine can draft a defence better than me for pennies, Kerr and Amadi can't afford me. I'd have no savings, no other legal jobs in town, and a loan I still owe for the degree that got me here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write to our MP the first week and join every campaign for a human right to representation. I'd give notice on my flat and move back into my mum's spare room in the next town to stop paying rent. I'd cut everything down to food, travel and my phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor drops away. I'm twenty-seven, I did everything right, and the career ladder disappears just as I reached the top of it. I'd be lying awake every night doing sums that don't work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the robot part comes three years later. Does that matter for your job at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. My job is thinking, talking and writing. The only part that's hands-on is standing up in court, and that's about rules, not robots. Courts might insist on a person for a bit longer, but I wouldn't bet my rent on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you be living by the end of 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In my mum's spare room with my case files in boxes, I expect. My mum works at the school kitchen and she'd make room without a word. I'd hate being a burden, but I'd hate an eviction notice of my own even more.

say: We need laws **guaranteeing a human lawyer** for anyone who might lose their home.
This is the moment **unions and governments** either step in or don't.
think: With **two years** of warning, I'm finished as a housing lawyer.
I'd have **no savings**, no other legal jobs in town, and a **student loan**.
do: Write to the **local MP** in the first week about a right to representation.
Give notice on the flat and **move back** to her mum's spare room.
Cut spending to **food, travel** and the phone.
feel: Like the **floor drops away** just as she reached the top.
**Sleepless**, doing sums that don't add up.
S2.quote: I'm twenty-seven, I did everything right, and the career ladder disappears just as I reached the top of it.
fieldNote: The **robot delay** gives her nothing, since nearly all her work is thinking work.
She reaches for **politics** first and family second, with no personal escape plan.
Moving home to her mum is the **safety net** she resents but would use.

steps.text: Write to the local MP about a right to a human lawyer
Give notice on the flat and move into her mum's spare room
Cut spending to food, bus fares and the phone

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Much the same as before, but more organised. I'd say the profession has five years to win a legal right to a human lawyer at eviction hearings, and we'd better start now. I'd be at every law society meeting saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years buys me time, but the same ending. I think the firm would last maybe three of those years, and then it's me against a machine that's cheaper and never sleeps. Courtroom work might hold on a little longer, so I'd want to be the person the court actually needs in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put a fixed amount away every month, even fifty a month, until I had three months saved. I'd get on the committee of the housing lawyers' group so I'm in the room when the rules get written. I'd take more hearings and less drafting, so my name is known at the court.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still frightening, but it's a slower kind of fear. Two years of warning felt like a cliff, and five years feels like a long hill down. I can at least plan the walk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could you do with five years that you couldn't with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, maybe. I'd still not touch the tools for my own drafting, but I'd learn enough to know how they get things wrong. That's useful when you're arguing against them in court.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you avoid new things. Would five years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi, my trainee, says I'm being stubborn. He might be right, but stubborn people are the ones who stay and argue for tenants when everyone else has left. I'd rather be that than nothing.

say: The profession has **five years** to win a right to a **human lawyer** at eviction hearings.
We should **organise now**, not when the machines are already in court.
think: Five years buys **time**, not a different ending.
**Courtroom work** might hold on longest, so I'd want to be needed in the room.
do: Save a **fixed amount** monthly until she has **three months** put by.
Join the **committee** of the housing lawyers' group.
Take on **more hearings** and less drafting.
feel: A slower fear, like a **long hill down** rather than a cliff.
S3.quote: Two years of warning felt like a cliff, and five years feels like a long hill down. I can at least plan the walk.
fieldNote: She shifts towards **court advocacy** as the part of her job a person might keep.
She'd learn about AI only to **argue against** it, not to use it.
Even small **savings** feel like a real plan to her.

steps.text: Save fifty a month until three months of costs are put by
Join the committee of the housing lawyers' group
Ask Daniel Kerr for more court hearings and less drafting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so let's use it to make sure no family loses their home because a machine argued their case. I'd want legal aid funded properly before AGI comes, not after. That's the message I'd push everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years gives me a real choice. I could move into the public sector, a council legal team or a funded law centre, where a human lawyer might be protected by law longer than at a private firm. I'd be thirty-seven when it lands, which is young enough to do something else if I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start applying for jobs at funded law centres and council legal teams in the city, even though it means a commute. I'd keep saving, slowly, and clear the credit card. I'd stay at Kerr and Amadi until something steady came up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but not calm. There's still the rent and the loan and the fact that my firm could lose its contract any spring. A decade means the AI worry joins the queue behind the money worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time at twenty-seven. Would you still be a lawyer in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes, but maybe in a different seat. I can picture being the person who checks what the machines decided, on behalf of tenants. It would still be housing law, just from another angle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your mum say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum would say I worry too much and should come home for Sunday dinner more. My mum cleaned offices for twenty years so I could do this, and she'd tell me nobody can take what's in my head. I'm not sure that's still true, but I'd love her for saying it.

say: We've got **a decade** to fund legal aid properly before AGI comes.
No family should lose their home because a **machine argued** their case.
think: Ten years lets me move to the **public sector**, where protection may last longer.
At **thirty-seven** I'd still be young enough to do something else.
do: Apply to **funded law centres** and council legal teams in the city.
Clear the **credit card** and keep saving slowly.
Stay at the firm until a **steady job** comes up.
feel: **Calmer** but not calm, with the AI worry queued behind **money worries**.
S4.quote: My mum cleaned offices for twenty years so I could do this, and she'd tell me nobody can take what's in my head.
fieldNote: Ten years turns her **fear into a plan**: a move to publicly funded work.
Her **existing money worries** keep her from feeling calm even here.
Her mum's **sacrifice** is a strong part of why she stays in law.

steps.text: Apply to funded law centres and council legal teams in the city
Pay off the credit card and keep saving monthly

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt, because I'd have no time and no money to do anything except move home. What would help is a law saying anyone facing eviction gets a human lawyer, paid for properly. I'd also need legal aid rates that let people like me save a little.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the tenants. Everyone talks about what AI does to lawyers, but a family in a damp flat can't argue with a chatbot that says the landlord is right. Ask them too.

headlineQuote: A family in a damp flat can't argue with a chatbot that says the landlord is right.
portrait: Grace leads the **housing team** at a small firm, defending tenants against eviction in a mill town.
She has **three weeks of savings**, a student loan, and rent eating half her pay.
She never uses **AI tools** and blames cost-cutting firms and government, not the technology.
Her fear rises from **anxious** in the calm pictures to **alarmed** when AGI comes fast.
Her answers are **campaigning**, moving home to her mum, and later a public-sector job.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, leaving no time or money except moving home.
whatWouldHelp: A legal right to a **human lawyer** for anyone facing eviction, properly funded.
**Legal aid rates** high enough for young lawyers to save a little.
